theory.intro: Faults in surveys, experiments and observations can make results unreliable. Check how answers are obtained, who is missing, whether comparisons are fair, and how measurements are recorded. Suggest changes that address the stated fault.
facts: The **interviewer effect** occurs when participants alter answers to please an interviewer or avoid embarrassment.
Identifiable answers to sensitive questions may discourage honest replies or participation. Explain how information is used and protect respondents from unnecessary identification.
**Non-response bias** is possible when people who reply differ from those who do not. Follow-ups can help, but cannot guarantee everyone replies.
A comparable **control group** without the tested treatment helps show whether a change would occur anyway. Keep other relevant conditions the same.
Other differences between groups may explain the results instead of the factor being tested. These are **confounding variables**.
**Measurement error** arises from uncalibrated or faulty instruments producing inaccurate readings.
Being watched may change behaviour: the **observer effect**. Asking people to remember details from long ago can cause **recall error**.
**Transcription errors** occur when manual mistakes are made transferring data into digital records.

workedExamples.question_text:
A school surveys students about bullying.
(a) A teacher reads each question aloud and asks students to identify themselves when answering. Explain a risk and suggest an improvement.
(b) Only 24 of 300 selected students return a confidential form. Explain why those replies alone may not describe all selected students.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Students may avoid revealing sensitive experiences when the teacher and other students can identify their answers. Let them complete a confidential form privately and avoid unnecessary identifying details. Explain how the information will be used.
(b) The students who replied may differ from those who did not. Contact selected non-respondents with suitable reminders and ways to answer. Do not assume their experiences match the 24 replies; follow-up does not guarantee full participation.

workedExamples.question_text:
A class tests whether a new plant feed improves seedling growth.
(a) All seedlings receive the feed and grow during the week. Why is the growth alone not enough to establish the feed caused it?
(b) The class adds untreated seedlings, but keeps the fed seedlings in sunlight and the untreated seedlings in shade. Explain the remaining fault.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Seedlings might grow during the week without the new feed. Include a comparable group without the feed to check this.
(b) The groups also differ in light. A growth difference could be caused by light rather than the feed. Keep light, water, plant type and the measurement period the same, so the feed is the factor being compared.

workedExamples.question_text:
A researcher studies usual walking behaviour.
(a) People are followed closely by a researcher taking notes. Explain how this may affect the observation.
(b) Other people are asked to remember their exact walking times from each day of the previous term. Explain the difficulty and suggest an improvement.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) People may alter how they walk when they notice they are being watched. The observation may not show usual behaviour. Use a less intrusive observation method while respecting participants' privacy.
(b) Exact times from long ago may not be remembered accurately. Record times as they occur using a consistent procedure, instead of reconstructing them from distant memory.

workedExamples.question_text:
A team collects temperature records.
(a) A thermometer gives a reading above the known temperature when checked. What should the team do before relying on it?
(b) A reading of 46 is entered in a spreadsheet as 64. Identify the error and suggest a check.
(c) The recorder omits every reading below a chosen threshold. Why can the record no longer describe all measured temperatures?
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Check the instrument against known temperatures, calibrate it if possible or replace it, and use the same checked procedure for the measurements. Otherwise the readings may be consistently inaccurate.
(b) The digits have been reversed during data entry: a transcription error. Compare the digital entry with the original record and correct it. Check other entries for the same kind of mistake.
(c) The record leaves out lower temperatures, so it does not cover the full set measured. Keep all valid readings and state how they were collected.

foundation.question_text:
A school principal stands in front of each classroom and asks students to raise their hands if they have ever cheated on an exam.
Identify the data collection fault.
foundation.solution_text:
Students may avoid admitting cheating in front of the principal because they fear consequences. Their answers are identifiable when they raise their hands.
Interviewer influence and lack of anonymity for a sensitive question.

foundation.question_text:
A scientist tests a new plant fertiliser on $20$ tomato plants in a greenhouse and observes that they grow $15\text{ cm}$ in a month.
No plants are grown without the fertiliser.
Identify the fault in the experimental design.
foundation.solution_text:
Without a control group of plants grown under identical conditions without fertiliser, there is no baseline to determine how much growth occurred naturally.
Lack of a control group.

foundation.question_text:
A nutrition researcher asks adults to recall the exact number of grams of protein and carbohydrates they consumed on each day over the past three months.
Identify the fault in this data collection method.
foundation.solution_text:
Adults may not accurately remember exact food and nutrient amounts from each day over three months. Guesses can make the recorded quantities unreliable.
Recall error in self-reported data.

foundation.question_text:
A study compares the effect of a new study technique by testing Group A in a quiet morning session at $21^{\circ}\text{C}$ and Group B in a noisy afternoon session at $32^{\circ}\text{C}$.
Identify the experimental fault.
foundation.solution_text:
Noise and temperature differed between the groups, introducing extraneous factors that influence test performance.
Inconsistent experimental conditions and confounding variables.

foundation.question_text:
A police department surveys community members about their trust in local officers by having uniformed officers conduct face-to-face door-to-door interviews.
State how to fix this data collection process to obtain truthful data.
foundation.solution_text:
Some residents may feel pressure to report trust when speaking directly to uniformed officers.
Use a confidential questionnaire completed without an officer watching, with no unnecessary identifying details. Provide suitable online and paper options. This reduces pressure but does not guarantee truthful answers.

foundation.question_text:
A workplace manager sits directly behind factory employees with a clipboard and stopwatch to record their standard daily work speed.
Explain why the recorded speeds may be inaccurate.
foundation.solution_text:
Employees may change their usual pace because they know management is watching. The recorded speed may therefore differ from their normal daily speed.
Observer effect; the direction of the change is not certain.

foundation.question_text:
A hospital surveys discharged patients by mailing $1000$ questionnaires.
Only $80$ patients reply, and the hospital records their responses without following up the remaining $920$ patients.
Identify the data collection fault.
foundation.solution_text:
$80$ of $1000$ replied, so $920$ did not: $\frac{920}{1000}\times100\%=92\%$.
The patients who replied may have different experiences from those who did not. Without follow-up, their answers alone may not represent all discharged patients.
High non-response and a risk of non-response bias.

development.question_text:
An athletic trainer tests a new sports drink on a running squad.
The trainer uses an electronic timing gate for the morning pre-test and a handheld manual stopwatch for the afternoon post-test.
Identify the data collection fault and explain its impact.
development.solution_text:
Switching between automatic timing gates and manual stopwatches introduces human reaction time error.
Instrument and measurement error, producing inconsistent timing measurements.

development.question_text:
A clinical trial tests a new headache medication by giving the active drug to $50$ patients and recording how many report pain relief after $1$ hour.
Describe what must be added to make this a valid experimental design.
development.solution_text:
Add a comparable control group whose patients do not receive the active medication, and measure pain relief after the same one-hour interval under the same conditions.
Compare the groups to help distinguish the medication effect from changes that might occur anyway.

development.question_text:
A research assistant manually types $5000$ handwritten numerical health surveys into a spreadsheet.
Upon auditing $50$ random entries, $8$ contain transposed digits (such as typing 81 instead of 18).
Identify the data collection fault.
development.solution_text:
Manual transcription of handwritten data leads to human typing mistakes.
Data-entry and transcription error.

development.question_text:
A researcher tests whether a memory supplement improves exam scores.
Group 1 receives the supplement and is composed of high-achieving university medical students.
Group 2 receives no supplement and is composed of primary school students.
Identify the critical fault in this study.
development.solution_text:
The groups differ in age, education and previous achievement before receiving the supplement. These differences could explain different exam scores.
Use comparable groups and the same test conditions; do not attribute their difference to the supplement alone.

development.question_text:
A survey on household income and personal debt is conducted by a bank loan officer who asks customers direct questions during mortgage interview meetings.
Explain why the collected income and debt data may be biased.
development.solution_text:
Applicants may overstate income or conceal informal debts to improve their chances of loan approval with the loan officer.
Interviewer effect and lack of anonymity in a high-stakes setting.

development.question_text:
A zoo studies chimpanzee social behaviour by having a researcher in bright clothing stand $1\text{ metre}$ from the enclosure cage taking notes, causing the animals to display agitation.
Propose a change to the observation process that removes this fault.
development.solution_text:
The visible presence of the researcher alters natural animal behaviour (observer effect).
Observe the animals via hidden remote cameras or from behind one-way observation glass.

development.question_text:
A traffic department studies speeding on a local road by counting only the vehicles stopped by police patrol cars, while vehicles that passed without incident are unrecorded.
Identify the fault in this observational record.
development.solution_text:
The record includes only vehicles stopped by police and leaves out vehicles that pass without being stopped. It cannot show the speeding behaviour of all traffic.
Missing and incomplete observational records; do not assume every stopped driver was speeding.

mastery.question_text:
A pharmaceutical company tests an energy supplement.
Participants in the treatment group take the supplement with coffee and are told it will boost their alertness. The comparison group receives no supplement, drinks water and is told they are untreated.
Both groups then rate their energy levels.
Identify two critical faults in this experimental procedure.
mastery.solution_text:
1. Telling the treatment group to expect greater alertness may influence their self-reported energy ratings. Use neutral instructions.
2. Coffee in one group and water in the other introduce another difference that could affect energy. Keep these conditions the same so the supplement is the factor being compared.

mastery.question_text:
A university conducts a study on student study hours using a single end-of-semester survey where students estimate their daily study time for every week of the 14-week semester.
Explain the primary fault and propose an accurate data-collection design.
mastery.solution_text:
Students may not accurately recall daily study time across all 14 weeks at the end of the semester.
Ask them to record study time as it occurs, with regular reminders or weekly checks, rather than reconstructing every day months later. The records should still be checked for omissions or mistakes.

mastery.question_text:
A company audits its workplace safety culture.
The safety officer interviews workers while the factory supervisor stands alongside them.
Workers who report minor safety breaches are asked to sign an acknowledgement form that is placed in their personnel file.
Identify two distinct data collection faults in this process and explain how each distorts the results.
mastery.solution_text:
1. The supervisor's presence may pressure workers to under-report breaches because they fear consequences.
2. Signed acknowledgements placed in personnel files make reports traceable to individuals, which may discourage honest reporting.
Collect feedback without the supervisor watching and protect sensitive reports from unnecessary identification.
